It was named by American explorer Admiral Richard E. Byrd in 1929 in honor of his wife, Marie Byrd.
The region is home to the Bentley Subglacial Trench, which, at 2,555 meters below sea level, is the lowest point on Earth not covered by an ocean (though it is covered by a massive layer of ice).
Because it is unclaimed, it is a popular setting for "micronations" created by internet enthusiasts, though none of these are internationally recognized.
Most of the region's volcanoes are subglacial, meaning they erupt underneath the ice sheet, which scientists believe could potentially accelerate ice melt from below.

12. In 1920, in the aftermath of the First World War, an unusual international treaty created one of the world's most remarkable legal anomalies. A remote arctic archipelago — strategically located, rich in coal, and previously a source of international contention — was placed under the sovereignty of one Nordic nation. But the treaty came with a condition without parallel in international law: citizens of any signatory nation could live and work on the islands indefinitely, with no visa requirement, no work permit, and no immigration restrictions of any kind. Today, more than 40 nations are signatories. The archipelago is technically part of one country — but open to most of the world.
